newsitem.title: UK: European sugar traders await Iraq tender result.
newsitem.headline: European sugar traders await Iraq tender result.

text.p: Results of Iraq's tender to buy up to 120,000 tonnes of sugar under the U.N. oil-for-food deal could take some time to emerge due to the complexity of the deal, sugar traders said on Tuesday.
European market sources said while they were still waiting for firmer news on the tender, details would be sketchy for some time.

Some trade sources said Iraq might have postponed the tender to February 28 and suggested that the required amount of sugar might be nearer 60,000 tonnes, not 120,000. No immediate confirmation was available.
Offers to sell sugar into Iraq are subject to strict supervision with letters of credit to be opened by the New York branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP).
"They can't ship it until they've got the LCs (letters of credit)...which comes from the Iraqi account with the BNP in New York," said one trader.
"They'll probably bid against all the offers they've got and then negotiate sales with trade houses but there's no guarantee anything is going to be shipped."
U.N. approval is usually sought within several days of a deal being finalised. The plan allows Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion to buy food and medicine.
The only firm news so far is that Turkey's state sugar refiner Turkseker is to offer Iraq 25,000 tonnes of whites after a December offer of 50,000 tonnes was rejected at $390 per tonne.

Traders said Thailand and the European Union were likely origins for the sugar which Iraq eventually buys, although new crop Brazil cargoes could also compete, depending on how long the U.N. takes to approve the sale.
French trade houses are believed to have sold some 50,000 tonnes of sugar into Iraq under the deal, although the total amount of sugar purchased to date is unclear.
Some traders have suggested a total figure of up to 150,000 tonnes.
But even before the U.N. deal was concluded, Iraq was buying sugar on the international black market, with small shipments coming through Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba, they said.
